The acting agent’s manual is one Markdown file, the same for every task; the interface.md of each enabled task tool is appended to it under the heading “Extra tools for this task”. It contains, in this order:

World frame. One right-handed frame for both arms and all cameras, in metres, degrees and seconds; origin on the floor between the arm bases, + x +x to the robot’s right, + y +y away from it, + z +z up; a nominal table top at z = 0.74 z{=}0.74 (the shared table_plane tool measures the real height, about 0.765); arm bases at x = ∓ 0.30 x{=}\mp 0.30 , y = − 0.45 y{=}-0.45 ; how the frame appears in the head image, with a top-view drawing.

Gripper. The TCP is the midpoint between the fingertips; the tool frame’s x x is the approach direction and y y the opening axis; gripper value 1 is fully open (8.8 cm), 0 closed, and only the commanded value is reported. A reach envelope: pointing straight down the TCP reaches about y = 0.00 y{=}0.00 at table height, pointing down45 about y = 0.15 y{=}0.15 .

Base commands. obs and status (free); move (translate the TCP along world axes, at most 0.20 m per axis), rotate (about the TCP in the world or tool frame, at most 90 ∘ 90^{\circ} per axis), point (down, forward or down45, with a required opening axis), gripper, home, wait (at most 5 s), each costing simulation time; done, which ends the episode.
Limits. 60 commands per episode; simulation time limited per task; “the simulation only runs while a command runs; thinking costs no simulation time”.

Feedback. One JSON object per command: the request, clipping and workspace flags, plan_ok with a failure reason (ik_unreachable, self_collision, table_collision, workspace_limit), the reached pose and its error, settled, the gripper value, the time used and left, the commands left, and episode_over; exit codes for argument errors, failed commands, a finished episode and client time-outs. Motion planning knows the arm and the table, not the objects.

Observations. Head and two wrist RGB images ( 640 × 480 640{\times}480 ) and state.json with both TCP poses, joint angles, gripper values, and each camera’s intrinsics and camera-to-world extrinsics, followed by the formulas that project a world point to a pixel and turn a pixel into a ray. There is no depth; the manual names the shared table_plane tool and the two ways to fix a point on a ray, a measured plane or a second view.

Rules. When the task is finished, home both arms and then call done; call done only when sure; read a failed command’s output before deciding; object positions are not given and must be worked out from the images and the calibration.

The optimizer receives a 62-line role description and, each round, a focus.md that selects one of three modes. In failure mode it reads the failure category, every command with its target, the reached pose, the acting agent’s trajectory and the head-camera frames; decides which perception tool, execution tool or repair would have prevented the failure, or that the failure was bad luck and nothing should change; implements it under tasks/ ⟨ \langle task ⟩ \rangle /tools/; enables it; and appends a dated entry to skill.md. In success mode it appends at most 15 lines to playbook.md and changes no tool unless one misbehaved. In final mode it rewrites playbook.md and skill.md (under 60 lines each) and every interface.md (under 12 lines). Six rules apply throughout: a tool may use only the EpisodeAPI (joint angles, TCP poses, motion primitives, the latest observation, the caller’s arguments) and must never read simulator state or hard-code layout-specific numbers; positions come from OpenCV geometry on the RGB images and the calibration, and no size, height or position of an object may come from the benchmark’s assets, layouts, configuration or logs; an interface.md describes the interface only and may not name the task or its objects, which the delivery check enforces with a list of banned words; the shared pool is read-only; tools validate their arguments, return a planning verdict like the base commands and never raise; and the optimizer runs no evaluations. Each round ends with a 3–10 line proposal.md.

Each evaluation seed is a directory of pre-sampled layouts, 30 to 75 per task. Within a seed, standard layouts differ only in the task objects’ positions and yaw (sampled inside per-object rectangles) and in the table and ground materials; random layouts additionally sample 13 to 18 distractor objects from 85 categories with their own poses. A few tasks vary content rather than pose: press by number keeps every object fixed and changes only the two digits; classify objects draws three objects from ten categories. The leaderboard takes the first 50 valid layouts of each seed; our development layouts are the first ten of seed 0.

In make toast the robot puts two of four bread slices from a rack into the two slots of a toaster and presses the lever down; full credit also requires exactly two slices left in the rack and the robot back at its origin. On test seed 0, layout 11, the agent without the skill asked the right arm to lift each slice at pitch 60 ∘ 60^{\circ} , a pose just out of its reach, and the arm went to the closest reachable pose, which, the tool noted, “tilts what it holds by 5 ∘ 5^{\circ} ” (cells 8 and 14). The second slice shifted in the fingers on its way down to the left slot; the descent stopped 13 mm short, where the hand opened and left the slice leaning (cells 15–16). While being straightened, it slipped out and fell flat beside the toaster (cell 39). A third slice from the rack took its slot (cells 60–63). The eleventh close on the fallen slice lifted it, at step 1,168, and the agent set it back in the rack. The episode ended at step 1,393 of 1,400, with the slice in the left slot tilted and a partial score of 25 ( Fig. 9 ).
(a) Cells 16–17: released where its descent stopped 13 mm short, the second slice leans across the left slot.
(b) Cells 39–40: the slice slips out while being straightened and falls flat beside the toaster, with 936 steps left.
(c) Cell 19: both slices, held at pitch 45 ∘ 45^{\circ} from rack to slot, stand edge-on in their slots.
(d) Cell 21: a closed hand presses the lever at pitch 30 ∘ 30^{\circ} ; success at step 222, during robot.home() .

Figure 9 : Make toast, test seed 0, layout 11: a leaning slice and two seated ones. Right wrist camera in (a), above the toaster, and in (c), above its lever; head camera in (b) and (d); all cropped. In both runs the first slice went into the right slot.

The skill, 65 lines without code, settles the carry before the first grasp. Dry runs are to find “ONE arm and pitch” that reach both a rack slice, with its lift of about 11 cm, and the slots, trying pitch 60 ∘ 60^{\circ} first, as in all three development successes, then 45 ∘ 45^{\circ} and 30 ∘ 30^{\circ} . It warns that “an offered pitch or yaw tilts or turns the held slice”, and that slices kept at the same pitch and roll from rack to slot stayed upright, “6/6 seated”. It also records that a lost slice is hard to make up for: “A flat slice was seated once in 44 low closes (6 runs)”, and a third slice from the rack, tried in four development runs, scored 0 in each.

With the skill, on the same layout, dry runs in cell 7 found that at pitch 60 ∘ 60^{\circ} the lift could only be approached, 7 ∘ 7^{\circ} off, while at 45 ∘ 45^{\circ} the grasp, the lift and the slot were all reachable. Both slices then stayed within 1 ∘ 1^{\circ} of pitch 45 ∘ 45^{\circ} and roll 0 ∘ 0^{\circ} from rack to slot and went in without a block (cells 8–19); success came during robot.home() at step 222 of 1,400. Over the 30 test episodes, successes rise from 15 to 21. In 14 of the 15 failures without the skill a slice fell, in 8 of them, as here, while the agent was correcting a slice that rested tilted, high or on the rim. With the skill, a slice slipped in each of the 9 failures as well. Three of the 4 episodes that passed only without the skill have cluttered layouts. There the agent with the skill judged the rack and the toaster too far apart for a steep carry with one arm, a case in which four development runs had all failed, and lost a slice carried at a pitch of 0 ∘ 0^{\circ} to 30 ∘ 30^{\circ} . Without the skill, the agent handed the slices between the arms, which the skill advises against: hand-overs passed none of 14 slices in the development runs. In the fourth, the second slice tipped the first during the carry.

In pack objects into box the robot puts a toy car, an electric toothbrush, a hammer and a shoe into an open box, each with its front to the left; full credit requires all four in “the aligned box” and a return to origin. On test seed 0, layout 14, the box stood about 20 ∘ 20^{\circ} off the table’s edges, and the agent without the skill wrote “I’ll straighten it before packing”. Its left hand gripped the near wall, lifted the box and turned it (cells 7–9), then again (cells 14–15). After the arm carrying the car shifted the box, the agent dragged it by the rim to the middle of the table (cells 23–24). There, picking up the shoe beside it tipped the box onto its end (cell 35); righting it took 242 steps (cells 38–50). The cells that handled the box took 500 of the 1,300 steps; the budget ran out at a score of 10, one item placed correctly ( Fig. 10 ).

(b) Cell 35: picking up the shoe beside it tips the box on end; righting it takes 242 steps.
(c) Cell 15: hammer, car and toothbrush have gone straight down from 0.95 m into the untouched box.

The skill, 63 lines without code, states what “aligned” meant in the development runs: “A tipped or far-turned box counts nothing (the card: aligned); shifted but upright, items counted (4 successes).” For a moved box it records “Gripping, hooking or dragging a moved box: 13 runs, none restored” and prescribes “Upright, roughly left-right, reachable: new centre, go on”. Since the two runs of each episode differ only in the skill, the success with it shows that the agent could perceive and handle the objects of that episode. What it lacked without the skill was a fact about the task, which the skill supplied in a few lines. The facts are of the three kinds named in Fig. 6 . Three are success conditions that the card leaves open: which tile to place and where it stands (make kong), which end of each pen goes up (fill pen holder) and when a moved box still counts as aligned (pack objects into box). One is a parameter that only contact reveals: a turn that pushes the nut down, with the measured heights that tell a seated nut from one on the tip (fasten screws). Two concern the ordering of steps: each pillar level is built from one pillar of each side (build tower), and the arm and pitch of the whole carry are settled by dry runs before the first slice is grasped (make toast). In five of the episodes, the agent without the skill spent its remaining steps on a repair that the skill rules out: straightening the box, turning the nut back and forth, moving the discard, taking apart the top of a tower whose lower pair could not be credited, and recovering a fallen slice while a third one took its slot. Each of these facts came from development runs in which an attempt succeeded or failed for a reason that the card does not state. The skills leave other failures in place. With the skill, fill pen holder still fails 14 times, each time with a highlighter that would not stay in the held holder; make toast fails 9 times, each time after a slice slipped; and the one failure of build tower stopped at a finished tower for a reason the record does not show. The make-toast skill also cost episodes: in three cluttered layouts, the agent with it carried each slice with one arm at a pitch of 0 ∘ 0^{\circ} to 30 ∘ 30^{\circ} and lost one, whereas the agent without it handed the slices between the arms, which the skill advises against, and succeeded.

On the code of round R0 and its 420 development episodes, we compared our system prompt with one taken from the manual of another open agent framework. Ours solved 223 episodes and the other 198, so we kept ours.

The model has two tools: python(code) runs one cell, and finish(status, summary) ends the episode. A reply may hold several cells, which run in order. The status of finish gives the reason: no_budget when the steps left cannot cover another attempt, stuck when there is no way forward, and keep_partial when another attempt would put a partial result at risk. The episode ends when the benchmark ends it, when the model calls finish , or at a limit on replies and time: 100 replies and 90 minutes on RoboDojo, and 40 replies (100 for RoboCasa365’s composite tasks) and two hours on the other benchmarks. The benchmark ends an episode on success, which it checks after every action, or when the step budget is spent. The scene is then judged as it stands. A step is one simulator action (0.04 s of simulated time on RoboDojo).

Pictures are sent as JPEG images. The model’s gateway accepts 8 to 10 MB per request, so only a window of pictures stays in the conversation. The start pictures on the task card are always kept. When the others pass 20 pictures or 8 MB, the oldest are replaced by a short placeholder until 14 remain. Two runs used a larger window ( Appendix A ). Dropping several pictures at once keeps the cached start of the conversation valid for longer. The loop also supports Claude models and open models served with vLLM.

Positions are in metres in the benchmark’s world frame and angles in degrees. Pixels are (column, row) from the top-left corner. Pitch 0 points the hand level and 90 points it straight down. Yaw turns the hand about the vertical and roll about its own axis. look attaches the current pictures to the cell’s result, optionally with a pixel grid, marked points, outlines, or an enlarged crop. The labels on a crop stay in full-picture pixels, so a pixel read off any picture can be passed to the other calls as it is.

A benchmark adds calls only where its robot can do more. On RoboCasa365 the base drives ( drive ), and doors and lids turn about their hinges ( arc , push_arc ). A helper there picks a round dish by its rim ( rim_pick ). LIBERO-PRO also has arc . Both benchmarks also hand the cell the raw depth picture ( depth ).

The design grew out of the task tools of HexaShell-TaskTools ( Section 3.4 ), which triangulated objects between calibrated RGB cameras inside each task’s own code. Here one service and one set of geometry serve every task, with depth where a benchmark renders it.

One SAM 3 service [ 14 ] runs on each machine and serves every episode there. A picture is uploaded once and then named by its hash. Words find by appearance only. Left or second do not pick an instance, so the model chooses among the masks by their centroids or points at the one it means.

RoboDojo has no depth camera, so measure works from outlines alone. A mask in one picture fixes a cone: the rays through its pixels, down to the table. To find the same object in another camera, the service is asked again, with the same words, or with clicks along the middle ray of the first outline at several heights above the table. Each candidate is scored by how well the two cones contain each other’s outline, and colour breaks near ties. The object then lies in the space that every camera able to see a point shows inside its outline, a visual hull that is probed along the pixels’ rays. Its top is the lowest height that still explains almost all outline pixels. Its footprint comes from the surface points each camera sees below the top. A rotated rectangle fitted to the footprint ( cv2.minAreaRect ) gives the object’s size and grip_yaw , the yaw that closes down-pointing fingers across its narrow side. Pixels that show the robot’s own arm do not count against an outline. They are found by drawing the arm’s meshes at the current joint readings. With one camera the height cannot be measured. The object is then taken to rest on its support, and the result says so and gives a wrist pose that would add a view.

to_world(cam, (x, y)) turns a pixel into a world point. A pixel fixes a ray, and the depth along it comes from one of three sources. The first is a horizontal plane at a height the model gives (a rim, a slot, the table). The second is the same point picked in a second picture: the two rays are intersected, and a gap of more than about 5 mm between them reveals a mismatch [ 34 ] . The third is the surface under the pixel. This is the table, a measured object, or a level patch that is matched between cameras by zero-mean normalized cross-correlation over candidate heights, a plane sweep [ 23 ] . Every result reports how far one pixel of picking error moves the point, and it warns when the pixel shows the robot’s own arm.

LIBERO-PRO and RoboCasa365 render a depth picture with every camera. There the same calls back-project a mask’s pixels through the depth picture and merge the points of all cameras that see the object. An oriented box on the floor plan gives the centre, size and grasp yaw, and the lowest and highest points give the height. Only the visible surface is measured, so when the cameras see an object from one side only, its centre leans toward them by up to half its depth. For pinch grasps, a circle fitted to the depth points around a round dish gives the outer edge of its rim. RoboTwin 2.0 renders depth as well, but in all our RoboTwin runs perception used only the colour pictures and the camera models, as on RoboDojo. On these three benchmarks the robot’s own pixels come from the renderer’s segmentation of the robot’s parts, not from its meshes.

Measured objects keep their id for the whole episode. Measuring an object again looks for it where it was last seen, or where the gripper has taken it, and falls back on its earlier height when only one camera sees it now. The RoboDojo prompt gives the model the errors to expect. From the start pictures, low box-like objects (blocks, tiles, small flat things) usually come out within a few millimetres. Round, hollow or tall objects (balls, bowls, cups, bottles) are often 1–3 cm off, and too high or too large rather than too low. A wrist camera held about 25 cm above the object, together with the head camera, brings the error to 1–2 mm. Pixels read from an enlarged crop are about twice as precise as pixels read from the whole picture.

On RoboDojo, HexaShell runs as a policy inside the benchmark’s own evaluation client, which asks for one action at a time. While the model thinks, the policy answers “wait”, so the simulation stands still and no step is used. On the other three benchmarks the simulator runs in a server process with its own Python environment and talks to HexaShell over a socket.

On RoboDojo and RoboTwin 2.0 the arms are ARX X5 arms and take joint targets. HexaShell solves inverse kinematics itself, with Levenberg–Marquardt steps on the 6-D pose error of the grasp point from several starting configurations. Of the solutions that keep the arm out of the table, it takes the one with the least joint travel. A straight path is solved waypoint by waypoint, and a swing is checked for table clearance along the way. Motions follow a trapezoid-like speed profile, so long moves across the table take fewer steps while the last centimetres of a descent stay slow. A short description of the rig (where the arms stand, where the table is, how the gripper reading relates to the fingers) lets the same driver serve both benchmarks.

On LIBERO-PRO and RoboCasa365 a Franka Panda runs under robosuite’s operational-space controller in delta mode. That controller lags a moving goal by about 0.16 s and does not compensate a held load. The adapter therefore plans a straight line on one speed profile and aims each step past the plan, by feeding forward the plan’s velocity and acceleration and slowly integrating what is left at rest. The same planner serves both benchmarks. On RoboCasa365 the arm also rides on a wheeled base.

The model’s cells run in a separate worker process with one persistent Python namespace, so variables and functions survive between cells. Every robot call is forwarded to the host process, which owns the arms, cameras and perception, and waits for the answer. After the worker has imported what it needs, it confines itself in three layers. Landlock limits file access to a few read-only trees (the Python installation, the HexaShell package and system libraries) and the worker’s own workspace, and it blocks every TCP connection. Seccomp forbids network sockets where Landlock cannot block them, new programs and processes, and signals to or tracing of other processes. At the Python level, imports are limited to a list of modules (numpy, math, cv2, json and similar) and open to the workspace. These last limits give clear error messages but are not the boundary. A cell may use a limited amount of CPU time; waiting for robot calls does not count. The simulator, the task code, the layouts, the skills’ sources and the network are therefore out of reach whatever a cell does.

Skills are written from the records of earlier runs and, where HexaShell-TaskTools had tools for a task, from what those tools had shown. Each claim carries its evidence. On the three newer benchmarks this is the number of episodes it was seen in, such as “(7 eps)”, or a mark for a probe, a scripted test, a HexaShell-TaskTools tool, or “untested”. RoboDojo skills name the development round and layouts instead, such as “R0 8/8” or “(l0)”. A checking script enforces the rules of Section 2.4 together with the format. On the three newer benchmarks a skill has at most 45 lines of 100 characters. On RoboTwin 2.0 the skills use only the instruction wording of the learning runs, never the unseen wording of the test. The RoboDojo skills went through four versions during the development rounds on layouts 0–9 of seed 0. The skills cite only learning and validation episodes.

The agent ends most failed episodes itself, and seldom early. On RoboDojo with skills it ended 125 of the 156 failures with finish , 99 of them because the steps left could not pay for another attempt, with a median of 22 steps left. The benchmark ended 28, nearly all at the step budget, and 3 reached the limit on replies or time. We count the episodes in which a motion raised Dropped . Without skills, 289 of the 1,019 episodes with a record had a slip; 28% of them still succeeded, against 80% of the episodes without one. With skills, 153 of the 1,020 had a slip (46% against 91%). The skills thus make slips rarer, through grasp heights and openings that held in earlier runs, and they help the agent recover from one, but a slip still costs much of the chance of success. With skills, 82 of the 156 failures had a slip, and 68 of these come from six tasks, led by store laptop and headphones (22 of its 29 failures) and hang mugs (13 of 23). The URAI adapter connects the API to two PiPER-X arms with a head camera and two wrist cameras, all RGB-D. URAI [ 32 ] , a separate service, plans and executes every motion: inverse kinematics, collision checking, time scaling and execution. For each goto the adapter sends URAI the target, asks for a planning-only preview of the whole trajectory, and executes it if the plan is accepted. With path="auto" it tries a straight line first. Otherwise it accepts a joint-space path only if the path stays within 3 cm of the line and no more than 1 cm below its end points. A refused plan raises NotExecuted as in simulation, and a grasp that closes on nothing raises Dropped . Steps are counted as executed time in units of 0.04 s, so a step budget buys about as much robot time as on RoboDojo.

The adapter has no segmentation service at present, so find , measure and things are absent. The model reads pixels off the pictures, with a grid or an enlarged crop, and to_world turns each pixel into a point. It uses the measured depth first, then a plane at a height the model gives, then a second view. The model checks a point by projecting it back with to_pixel and marking it in a new picture. The robot’s own pixels come from URAI’s collision capsules, projected into each picture and compared with the measured depth.

The real-robot prompt keeps the six parts of Section 2.3 in 11,110 characters of English. A real robot has no checker, so finish has one more status, done . The model’s report is stored with the episode. The adapter has 907 lines. The loop, the sandbox and the geometry of to_world above it are the code that runs the simulated benchmarks. The adapter’s 29 end-to-end tests pass against URAI’s kinematic simulator.
